name: Erik Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Erik. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to tech firms, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm 27 and I'm a marketing specialist at Brookvale Dairy, a regional yoghurt and milk brand, in a team of four. I get in at half eight, check how last week's posts and emails did, then spend most of the day writing: pack copy for the yoghurt pots, the monthly newsletter, ideas for the spring campaign. Gillian, my manager, signs everything off, and I eat lunch with Pete from the design desk most days.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like finding the one line that makes a pot of strawberry yoghurt sound like a Sunday morning. I'm proud when I see my words in the supermarket fridge. What wears me out is the pay and the spreadsheets: I'm on the lower end for this job, and Noor, my partner, and I have less than a month's rent saved. Brookvale got bought by a bigger dairy group last year, and since then everything is about cost savings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools in your work at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, never. Gillian set up a writing tool for the team last spring and I've not touched it. I write my own lines, the same way I learned at university, and I don't trust something that copies everyone else's words and calls it new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the tools stay a bit useless. Honestly, that sounds fine to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've always said: good copy comes from people who know the product and the customer. I'd probably post something like, see, the hype didn't hold up. Pete would laugh at me for being smug about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm still not safe. The new owners want savings whether AI works or not, and I'm the one person on the team who won't use Gillian's writing tool. If they ever cut one of us four, being the stubborn one doesn't help me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep writing the way I do, but I'd try to get more of my campaigns into the numbers so my work is easy to defend at review time. I'd ask the union for creative workers about joining, because there's nothing like that at Brookvale. And Noor and I would keep the food shop to sixty a week so we can put something aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly, but it's thin relief. The rent on our flat above the launderette on Station Road went up again in September, and that worry doesn't care about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try to get your work into the numbers. What does that look like on a Monday morning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start keeping a little sheet of which subject lines got people to open the newsletter, and which pack lines I wrote before a product sold better. Gillian loves a chart. If the group ever asks what I do, I want my manager Gillian to have a page she can wave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if one of the four of you did go, even in this calm picture, where would you look for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard part. The only agencies are in the city, an hour and a half on the train, and the fare would eat a big chunk of my pay. Around here, a marketing job opens maybe twice a year.

say: I'd say **good copy** still comes from people who know the product and the customer.
I'd joke that the **hype** didn't hold up and I was right not to bother.
think: I think the new owners want **cost savings** anyway, so my job is not safe.
I worry that refusing the **writing tool** makes me the easy one to cut.
do: Keep a simple **results sheet** on newsletters and pack lines from next month.
Ask about joining a **creative workers' union**, since Brookvale has none.
Hold the weekly **food shop** to sixty to save a little.
feel: I feel **relief** that the tools stay weak, but it is **thin relief**.
The **rent rise** on our flat still sits on my chest.
S0.quote: If the group ever asks what I do, I want my manager Gillian to have a page she can wave.
fieldNote: Even with AI fading, his **real worry** is the new owner chasing savings, not the technology.
He sees his **refusal** to use the tool as a risk, but won't change it.
Few **local jobs**: the nearest agencies are 90 minutes away by train.

steps.text: Keep a results sheet on newsletter subject lines and pack copy
Ask a creative workers' union about joining this winter
Hold the weekly food shop to sixty with Noor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and planning first. That's my whole job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: companies are using AI to cut wages and calling it progress. I'd share the posts from writers who've lost contracts. At work I'd ask Gillian straight out what the plan is for the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the group cuts us from four to two within a couple of years, and I'm not the one they keep. The person who stays will be the one who makes the AI churn out forty versions of a yoghurt line before lunch. That isn't me, and I don't know if I can make it me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union properly and push for a say in how the tool gets used. I'd probably have to sit down with Pete and let him show me the writing tool, which I hate saying. I'd also start looking at the council's marketing and communications jobs, because public sector posts feel steadier. And we'd cancel the streaming services and the gym straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like watching the tide come in while I'm still building a sandcastle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you don't trust the tool. If Pete sat you down with it, what would you actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch, and I'd probably use it for the boring bits, like the twenty little product descriptions for the website. I'd still write the main campaign line myself. Maybe that's the deal I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if your job went this way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not Gillian; she's squeezed too. I'd blame the group's owners and the tech companies selling them this, and a government that let it happen with no rules. There should be a law that says if a firm cuts jobs for AI, it pays for people to retrain.

say: I'd say firms use AI to **cut wages** and call it progress.
I'd ask my manager openly what the **plan for the team** is.
think: I think the team shrinks from **four to two** and I'm not kept.
The person kept will be the one who makes the AI **produce fast**.
do: Join the **union** properly and push for a say on the tool.
Let Pete show me the **writing tool** for small website descriptions.
Apply for **council communications** jobs and cancel streaming and gym.
feel: I feel **sick**, like watching the tide come in on a sandcastle.
S1.quote: The person who stays will be the one who makes the AI churn out forty versions of a yoghurt line before lunch.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** within two years and says so plainly.
His values push him toward the **union and regulation**, not toward the tool.
He'd grudgingly use AI for **small tasks** but guard the main campaign line.
Blames **owners, tech firms** and lack of rules, not his manager.

steps.text: Join the creative workers' union and ask for a say on tools
Use the writing tool for the twenty website product descriptions
Apply for council communications jobs in the spring round
Cancel the streaming services and the gym membership

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not even enough time to finish a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a crisis, and the government needs to step in with real money for people like me. I'd be at every protest going. Online I'd stop being polite about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm finished in marketing by 2028. If the AI can do any thinking work, a yoghurt brand doesn't need a copywriter at all, and I'd be out with less than a month's money saved. The robots come later, around 2031, so the only safe work for a few years is work with your hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start asking now about hands-on jobs: the dairy's own packing floor, delivery driving, anything with shifts. I'd ask Noor if we could move in with her mum for a while to stop paying rent. I'd sign on for whatever support exists the day I'm let go. And I'd be with the union, pushing for payouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. I don't have a plan, and I don't have the money to make one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the packing floor. What would that mean for you, day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Early shifts, standing all day. I'd be putting lids on the same yoghurt pots I used to write about, and knowing a robot is coming for that job by 2031. I'd still do it, because rent doesn't wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Noor's mum when you asked to move in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth: that we've got three weeks of money and I've got no job. She'd say yes, she always does. It's the asking that would hurt.

say: I'd call it a **crisis** and demand real government money for workers.
I'd go to **protests** and stop being polite online.
think: I think I'm **finished in marketing** by 2028, with under a month saved.
Only **hands-on work** is safe until robots come around 2031.
do: Ask about **packing floor** shifts and delivery work straight away.
Move in with **Noor's mum** to stop paying rent.
Sign on for **state support** and push the union for payouts.
feel: I feel like the **floor's gone**, with no plan and **no money** to make one.
S2.quote: I'd be putting lids on the same yoghurt pots I used to write about, and knowing a robot is coming for that job by 2031.
fieldNote: The short warning leaves him **no plan** and no savings to build one.
He sees **packing floor** work as a three-year stopgap before robots.
Moving in with **family** is his main fallback, and asking for it hurts his pride.

steps.text: Ask Brookvale's packing floor manager about early shifts
Move in with Noor's mum to stop paying rent
Sign on for state job-loss support the day he's let go
Push the union for redundancy payouts for marketing staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more than nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be pushing hard for rules now: a tax on firms that replace staff, and money for retraining. I'd say we've got five years and no excuse to waste them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it still means my job goes, around 2031. The difference is I'd have time to get into something else before it does. Five years is long enough to learn a trade, if I can afford to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for an evening course in something hands-on that robots reach late, maybe electrical work, since the robots only come around 2034. I'd keep my job at Brookvale while I study, and try to save fifty a month, which is about all we can manage. And I'd stay active in the union so the redundancy terms are decent when it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but at least it's the kind of scared that gets you moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Electrical work is a big change from copywriting. What draws you to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle Sami is an electrician, and he's never been out of work a day in his life. I always thought it was beneath what I studied. Now I think it might be the thing that keeps the lights on, literally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fifty a month. What gives, to find that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways, mostly, and the trip we'd planned to see Noor's cousins. That trip was the one thing we were looking forward to next year.

say: I'd push for a **tax on firms** that replace staff with AI.
I'd say five years leaves **no excuse** to do nothing.
think: I think my job still **goes around 2031**, just later.
Five years is enough to **learn a trade** if I can afford it.
do: Start an **evening course** in electrical work while keeping my job.
Save **fifty a month** by cutting takeaways and a family trip.
Stay active in the **union** for decent redundancy terms.
feel: I feel **scared**, but the kind of scared that **gets me moving**.
S3.quote: My uncle Sami is an electrician, and he's never been out of work a day in his life.
fieldNote: The **extra three years** turn panic into a plan to learn a trade.
He's dropping his old view that **trades** were beneath his degree.
Even saving **fifty a month** costs the couple their one planned trip.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening electrical course while still at Brookvale
Save fifty a month by cutting takeaways and the planned trip
Keep pushing the union for fair redundancy terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a whole career away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade to do this properly, so let's have the laws and the training money in place before anyone gets hurt. I'd get involved in local campaigns about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's still the end of what I do. But with ten years, I could finish an apprenticeship and be a qualified electrician before the thinking AI even arrives. That's a real plan, not a scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Brookvale for now and start the electrical course next autumn. I'd ask Sami if I could help on his jobs at weekends, for experience and a bit of cash. I'd vote for whoever promises retraining money, and I'd tell the union to start bargaining for it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, but it's a sad sort of calm. I'm grieving a job I actually like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss most about the writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing my line on a pot in the fridge at the supermarket and nudging Noor. Nobody will ever point at a light switch I wired and say, that's lovely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could make you stay in marketing, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the rules said a person had to sign off every advert, maybe. I'd fight for that. But I wouldn't bet our rent on it.

say: I'd say a decade gives time for **laws and training** money first.
I'd join **local campaigns** on how AI is brought in.
think: I think it's still the **end of copywriting** for me.
Ten years is enough to **qualify as an electrician** first.
do: Start the **electrical course** next autumn while staying at Brookvale.
Help my uncle Sami at **weekends** for experience and cash.
Vote for **retraining money** and push the union to bargain now.
feel: I feel **calmer**, but it's a **sad calm**, like grieving a job I like.
S4.quote: Nobody will ever point at a light switch I wired and say, that's lovely.
fieldNote: With ten years he has a **real plan**, which lowers his fear a lot.
His sadness is about losing **meaningful work**, not just income.
He'd still **fight for rules** but won't bet his rent on them.

steps.text: Start the electrical course next autumn while staying at Brookvale
Help his uncle Sami on electrical jobs at weekends for cash
Vote for parties promising retraining money
Ask the union to bargain now for retraining money

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because there's no time and we've got no money. What would help is a year's pay while I retrain, paid by the firms that cut us, and somewhere cheap to live while I do it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who's going to write the adverts for the robots. I'm half joking. I mean that people like me are being told to be flexible by people who've never had less than a month in the bank.

headlineQuote: People like me are being told to be flexible by people who've never had less than a month in the bank.
portrait: Erik is a **27-year-old copywriter** at a regional yoghurt brand, earning low pay with under a month saved.
He has **never used AI** and is proud of writing every line himself.
He leans left and blames **owners and tech firms**, wanting unions and laws to protect workers.
His mood runs from **anxious** in the calm picture to **panicked** when AGI comes in two years.
With more warning he would **retrain as an electrician**, like his uncle Sami.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there is no time and the couple has no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **year's pay** while retraining, paid by the firms that cut jobs.
**Cheap housing** while he learns a new trade.
